caption: Table 2-1. Data attributes and associated decision paths
context: As we've just seen, modeling strategies depend heavily on the data at hand. Table 2-1 provides a range of decision paths given our data volume and quality, based on our experience.
text:
Table 2-1. Data attributes and associated decision paths

Data attribute: Large data volume; Decision path: Can use techniques that require more data, like DL. Can use a richer set of features as well. If the data is sufficiently large but unlabeled, we can also apply unsupervised techniques.; Examples: If we have a lot of reviews and metadata associated with them, we can build a sentiment-analysis tool from scratch.
Data attribute: Small data volume; Decision path: Need to start with rule-based or traditional ML solutions that are less data hungry. Can also adapt cloud APIs and generate more data with weak supervision. We can also use transfer learning if there's a similar task that has large data.; Examples: This often happens at the start of a completely new project.
Data attribute: Data quality is poor and the data is heterogeneous in nature; Decision path: More data cleaning and pre-processing might be required.; Examples: This entails issues like code mixing (different languages being mixed in the same sentence), unconventional language, transliteration, or noise (like social media text).
Data attribute: Data quality is good; Decision path: Can directly apply off-the-shelf algorithms or cloud APIs more easily.; Examples: Legal text or newspapers.
Data attribute: Data consists of full-length documents; Decision path: Choose the right strategy for breaking the document into lower levels, like paragraphs, sentences, or phrases, depending on the problem.; Examples: Document classification, review analysis, etc.

caption: Table 2-2. Popular metrics and NLP applications where they're used
context: Table 2-2 lists various metrics used for intrinsic evaluation across various NLP tasks. For a more detailed discussion of the metrics, refer to the corresponding reference.
text:
Table 2-2. Popular metrics and NLP applications where they're used

Metric: Accuracy [48]; Description: Used when the output variable is categorical or discrete. It denotes the fraction of times the model makes correct predictions as compared to the total predictions it makes.; Applications: Mainly used in classification tasks, such as sentiment classification (multiclass), natural language inference (binary), paraphrase detection (binary), etc.
Metric: Precision [48]; Description: Shows how precise or exact the model's predictions are, i.e., given all the positive (the class we care about) cases, how many can the model classify correctly?; Applications: Used in various classification tasks, especially in cases where mistakes in a positive class are more costly than mistakes in a negative class, e.g., disease predictions in healthcare.
Metric: Recall [48]; Description: Recall is complementary to precision. It captures how well the model can recall positive class, i.e., given all the positive predictions it makes, how many of them are indeed positive?; Applications: Used in classification tasks, especially where retrieving positive results is more important, e.g., e-commerce search and other information-retrieval tasks.
Metric: F1 score [49]; Description: Combines precision and recall to give a single metric, which also captures the trade-off between precision and recall, i.e., completeness and exactness. F1 is defined as (2 × Precision × Recall) / (Precision + Recall).; Applications: Used simultaneously with accuracy in most of the classification tasks. It is also used in sequence-labeling tasks, such as entity extraction, retrieval-based questions answering, etc.
Metric: AUC [48]; Description: Captures the count of positive predictions that are correct versus the count of positive predictions that are incorrect as we vary the threshold for prediction.; Applications: Used to measure the quality of a model independent of the prediction threshold. It is used to find the optimal prediction threshold for a classification task.
Metric: MRR (mean reciprocal rank) [50]; Description: Used to evaluate the responses retrieved given their probability of correctness. It is the mean of the reciprocal of the ranks of the retrieved results.; Applications: Used heavily in all information-retrieval tasks, including article search, e-commerce search, etc.
Metric: MAP (mean average precision) [51]; Description: Used in ranked retrieval results, like MRR. It calculates the mean precision across each retrieved result.; Applications: Used in information-retrieval tasks.
Metric: RMSE (root mean squared error) [48]; Description: Captures a model's performance in a real-value prediction task. Calculates the square root of the mean of the squared errors for each data point.; Applications: Used in conjunction with MAPE in the case of regression problems, from temperature prediction to stock market price prediction.
Metric: MAPE (mean absolute percentage error) [52]; Description: Used when the output variable is a continuous variable. It is the average of absolute percentage error for each data point.; Applications: Used to test the performance of a regression model. It is often used in conjunction with RMSE.
Metric: BLEU (bilingual evaluation understudy) [53]; Description: Captures the amount of n-gram overlap between the output sentence and the reference ground truth sentence. It has many variants.; Applications: Mainly used in machine-translation tasks. Recently adapted to other text-generation tasks, such as paraphrase generation and text summarization.
Metric: METEOR [54]; Description: A precision-based metric to measure the quality of text generated. It fixes some of the drawbacks of BLEU, such as exact word matching while calculating precision. METEOR allows synonyms and stemmed words to be matched with the reference word.; Applications: Mainly used in machine translation.
Metric: ROUGE [55]; Description: Another metric to compare quality of generated text with a reference text. As opposed to BLEU, it measures recall.; Applications: Since it measures recall, it's mainly used for summarization tasks where it's important to evaluate how many words a model can recall.
Metric: Perplexity [56]; Description: A probabilistic measure that captures how confused an NLP model is. It's derived from the cross-entropy in a next-word prediction task. The exact definition can be found at [56].; Applications: Used to evaluate language models. It can also be used in language-generation tasks, such as dialog generation.

caption: Table 2-3. Project attribute and associated decision paths
context: As a start, Table 2-3 gives some guidance on how to approach the model updating process for different post-deployment scenarios.
text:
Table 2-3. Project attribute and associated decision paths

Project attribute: More training data is generated post-deployment.; Decision paths: Once deployed, extracted signals can be used to automatically improve the model. Can also try online learning to train the model automatically on a daily basis.; Examples: Abuse-detection systems where users flag data.
Project attribute: Training data is not generated post-deployment.; Decision paths: Manual labeling could be done to improve evaluation and the models. Ideally, each new model has to be manually built and evaluated.; Examples: A subset of a larger NLP pipeline with no direct feedback.
Project attribute: Low model latency is required, or model has to be online with near-real-time response.; Decision paths: Need to use models that can be inferred quickly. Another option is to create memoization strategies like caching or have substantially bigger computing power.; Examples: Systems that need to respond right away, like any chatbot or an emergency tracking system.
Project attribute: Low model latency is not required, or model can be run in an offline fashion.; Decision paths: Can use more advanced and slower models. This can also help in optimizing costs where feasible.; Examples: Systems that can be run on a batch process, like retail product catalog analysis.

caption: Table 2-4. Language attribute and action plan
context: We've compiled some action points for dealing with different languages in Table 2-4, based on our experiences working on projects that involve non-English language processing.
text:
Table 2-4. Language attribute and action plan

Language attribute: High-resource languages; Example and languages: Languages that have both ample data as well as pre-built models. Examples include English, French, and Spanish.; Action: Possible to use pre-trained DL models. Easier to use.
Language attribute: Low-resource languages; Example and languages: Languages that have limited data and recent digital adoption. May not have pre-built models. Examples include Swahili, Burmese, and Uzbek.; Action: Depending on the task, may need to label more data as well as explore individual components.
Language attribute: Morphologically rich; Example and languages: Linguistic and grammatical information like subject, object, predicate, tense, and mode are not separate words, but are joined together. Examples include Latin, Turkish, Finnish, and Malayalam.; Action: If the language is not resource rich, we'll need to explore morphological analyzers that exist for the language. In the worst case, manual rules to handle certain cases might be needed.
Language attribute: Vocabulary variation heavy; Example and languages: Nonstandard spellings and high word variation. For Arabic and Hindi, the spellings are nonstandard.; Action: If the language is not resource rich, then we may need to first normalize the words/spellings before training any model. This may not be needed for languages with large datasets, as they can still learn of vocabulary variation.
Language attribute: CJK languages; Example and languages: These languages are derived from ancient Chinese characters. They're not alphabet based and have several thousand characters for basic literacy and over 40,000 characters for larger coverage. Thus, they have to be handled differently. They include Chinese, Japanese, and Korean, hence the name CJK.; Action: Use specific tokenization schemes in these languages. Given that an ample amount of CJK data is available, it's possible to build NLP models for various tasks from scratch. There are also pre-trained models for them. Transfer learning from models trained in other languages beyond CJK may not be useful in this case.

caption: Table 4-1. Potential reasons for poor classifier performance
context: These are summarized in Table 4-1, and we'll look into some of them as we progress in this chapter.
text:
Table 4-1. Potential reasons for poor classifier performance

row_header: Reason 1; value: Since we extracted all possible features, we ended up in a large, sparse feature vector, where most features are too rare and end up being noise. A sparse feature set also makes training hard.
row_header: Reason 2; value: There are very few examples of relevant articles (~20%) compared to the non-relevant articles (~80%) in the dataset. This class imbalance makes the learning process skewed toward the non-relevant articles category, as there are very few examples of “relevant” articles.
row_header: Reason 3; value: Perhaps we need a better learning algorithm.
row_header: Reason 4; value: Perhaps we need a better pre-processing and feature extraction mechanism.
row_header: Reason 5; value: Perhaps we should look to tuning the classifier's parameters and hyperparameters.

caption: Table 6-2. Goal-oriented datasets from various domains and their usage
context: Table 6-2 is a brief summary of various datasets that are used for benchmarking algorithms for goal-oriented dialog tasks. As we're interested in various NLU tasks in dialogs, we present four datasets for goal-oriented dialogs that act as benchmarks for dialog-based NLU tasks.
text:
Table 6-2. Goal-oriented datasets from various domains and their usage

Dataset: ATIS [13]; Domain: Air Ticket Booking; Usage: Benchmark for intent classification and slot filling. This is a single-domain dataset, hence entities and intents are restricted to one domain.
Dataset: SNIPS [14]; Domain: Multidomain; Usage: Benchmark for intent classification and slot filling. This is a multidomain dataset, hence the entities belong to multiple domains. Multiple-domain datasets are challenging to model due their variability.
Dataset: DSTC [15]; Domain: Restaurants; Usage: Benchmark for dialog state tracking or joint determination of intent and slots. This is similarly a single-domain dataset, but the entities are expressed more in terms of annotations and contain more metadata.
Dataset: MultiWoZ [16]; Domain: Multidomain; Usage: Benchmark for dialog state tracking or joint determination of intent and slots that spans over multiple domains. For the similar reason of variability, modeling this dataset is more challenging than modeling single-domain ones.
